claim: The beta rhythm consists of oscillations in the 13–30 Hz range.
source: The beta rhythm consists of oscillations in the 13–30 Hz range.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the beta rhythm frequency range, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The motor cortex was found to be one of the main locations of beta rhythm in early recordings in human subjects.
source: The motor cortex was found to be one of its main locations in early recordings in human subjects (Jasper and Penfield, 1949; Penfield, 1954).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical research papers by Jasper and Penfield (1949) and Penfield (1954).

claim: Beta rhythm was recorded in cats during motionless focused attention when fixating a mouse behind a transparent screen.
source: It was recorded in cats during motionless focused attention, when fixating a mouse behind a transparent screen (Bouyer et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bouyer et al., 1987.

claim: Beta oscillations develop in the motor and premotor cortex during the movement preparatory period and wane during the movement itself in monkeys trained to perform an instructed-delay-task.
source: Subsequent studies in monkeys trained to perform an instructed-delay-task (Murthy and Fetz, 1992; Sanes and Donoghue, 1993) showed that beta oscillations develop in the motor and premotor cortex during the movement preparatory period and wane during the movement itself, in agreement with earlier observations in human (Jasper and Penfield, 1949; Penfield, 1954).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Murthy and Fetz, 1992; Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Jasper and Penfield, 1949; Penfield, 1954).

claim: Beta oscillations appear as synchronized bursts of a few cycles of oscillations, often synchronized on electrodes 1–2 mm apart.
source: It was also noted that beta oscillations did not have a constant amplitude in time but rather appeared as synchronized bursts of a few cycles of oscillations, often synchronized on electrodes 1–2 mm apart.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from previous research, implicitly citing earlier work mentioned in the context.

claim: Beta oscillations can come as planar or more complex waves propagating horizontally on the motor cortex.
source: More recently, it was observed using multi-electrode arrays that beta oscillations can come as planar (Rubino et al., 2006) or more complex (Rule et al., 2018; Denker et al., 2018) waves propagating horizontally on the motor cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rubino et al., 2006; Rule et al., 2018; and Denker et al., 2018.

claim: The model is based on recurrent interaction between local populations of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations of neurons coupled by longer range excitation.
source: The model is based on recurrent interaction between local populations of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations of neurons coupled by longer range excitation.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure developed in this study.

claim: The local E-I module is well-known to exhibit oscillatory dynamics when the recurrent interaction within the E population is sufficiently strong.
source: The local E-I module is well-known to exhibit oscillatory dynamics when the recurrent interaction within the E population is sufficiently strong.
evidence: This statement refers to established knowledge in computational neuroscience about E-I network dynamics.

claim: Long-range excitation between local E-I modules has been shown in previous works to synchronize the oscillatory dynamics of local E-I modules.
source: Long-range excitation between these local modules has been shown in previous works to synchronize the oscillatory dynamics of local E-I modules (Ermentrout and Kopell, 1991; Kulkarni et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ermentrout and Kopell, 1991 and Kulkarni et al., 2020.

claim: The whole network is close to the oscillation threshold.
source: Comparison with recordings leads us to propose that the whole network is close to the oscillation threshold and that fluctuating inputs from other cortical areas or other structures, such as the thalamus, power the burst of beta oscillations.
evidence: This is a proposal based on comparison with experimental recordings, representing an inference from data analysis.

claim: Fluctuating inputs from other cortical areas or other structures, such as the thalamus, power the burst of beta oscillations.
source: Comparison with recordings leads us to propose that the whole network is close to the oscillation threshold and that fluctuating inputs from other cortical areas or other structures, such as the thalamus, power the burst of beta oscillations.
evidence: This is a proposal based on comparison with experimental recordings and model behavior.

claim: The spatially extended network submitted to both local and global external inputs exhibits waves of different types that closely resemble those recorded in monkey motor cortex.
source: We show that such a spatially extended network submitted to both local and global external inputs exhibits waves of different types that closely resemble those recorded in monkey motor cortex.
evidence: This claim is based on model simulations compared to experimental data.

claim: The basal ganglia display prominent beta oscillations during different phases of movement.
source: On the one hand, the basal ganglia display prominent beta oscillations during different phases of movement (Leventhal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leventhal et al., 2012.

claim: Sources of beta oscillations have been identified in the cortex.
source: On the other hand, sources of beta oscillations have been identified in the cortex (Jensen et al., 2005; Sherman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jensen et al., 2005 and Sherman et al., 2016.

claim: Different cortical regions have intrinsic oscillation frequencies matching those of their prominent rhythms as supported by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) perturbation studies.
source: That different cortical regions have intrinsic oscillation frequencies matching those of their prominent rhythms is also supported by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) perturbation studies.
evidence: This statement refers to evidence from TMS studies, representing established experimental findings.

claim: The premotor area/supplementary motor area 6 has been found to resonate at ∼30 Hz after stimulation by a short TMS pulse.
source: Specifically, the premotor area/supplementary motor area 6 has been found to resonate at ∼30 Hz after stimulation by a short TMS pulse (Rosanova et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rosanova et al., 2009.

claim: Beta oscillations are generated by recurrent interactions in the motor cortex but are strongly modulated by inputs from other cortical areas or other structures, notably thalamic ones.
source: We thus adopt the intermediate view, previously advocated by Sherman et al., 2016, that beta oscillations are generated by recurrent interactions in the motor cortex but are strongly modulated by inputs from other cortical areas or other structures, notably thalamic ones.
evidence: This is a theoretical position adopted by the authors, supported by citation to Sherman et al., 2016.

claim: During the preparatory period of movement when beta oscillations are prominent, neurons do not fire periodically.
source: Here, one important observation is that during the preparatory period of movement when beta oscillations are prominent, neurons do not fire periodically.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data analysis.

claim: Isolated units from the recordings of Brochier et al., 2018 display large CVs.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, isolated units from the recordings of Brochier et al., 2018 display large CVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b from Brochier et al., 2018.

claim: Beta oscillations appear to be a collective phenomenon arising from sparse synchronization of different non-oscillating units.
source: Beta oscillations thus appear to be a collective phenomenon arising from sparse synchronization (Brunel and Hakim, 2008) of different non-oscillating units.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of large CVs, with citation to Brunel and Hakim, 2008 for the concept of sparse synchronization.

claim: Oscillations can emerge from recurrent interaction between interneurons when inhibition is sufficiently strong, but their frequencies tend to be in the upper gamma range or higher.
source: In such a regime, oscillations can emerge from recurrent interaction between interneurons, when inhibition is sufficiently strong. However, their frequencies are mainly controlled by the kinetics of synaptic transmission and tend to be in the upper gamma range or higher (Brunel and Wang, 2003; Geisler et al., 2005; de Solages et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brunel and Wang, 2003; Geisler et al., 2005; and de Solages et al., 2008.

claim: Lower frequencies arise in networks of E-I units, in which each of the two populations inhibits itself via a slower disynaptic loop.
source: Lower frequencies arise in networks of E-I units, in which each of the two populations inhibits itself via a slower disynaptic loop.
evidence: This is a statement about network dynamics based on established computational neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Beta oscillations are sparsely synchronized oscillations arising from recurrent interaction between excitatory and inhibitory populations.
source: This leads us to assume that beta oscillations are sparsely synchronized oscillations arising from recurrent interaction between excitatory and inhibitory populations.
evidence: This is an assumption made by the authors based on the preceding reasoning.

claim: The connection probability decreases with distance between neurons under different electrodes.
source: We assume that neurons under different electrodes are mainly connected by excitatory connections and that the connection probability decreases with distance (Huntley and Jones, 1991; Capaday et al., 2009; Hao et al., 2016).
evidence: This assumption is supported by citations to Huntley and Jones, 1991; Capaday et al., 2009; and Hao et al., 2016.

claim: The model consists of multiple recurrently coupled modules of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) neuron populations coupled by long-range excitatory connections.
source: It consists of multiple recurrently coupled modules of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) neuron populations. These local modules are further coupled by long-range excitatory connections.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The different modules are placed on a square 24 × 24 grid with the central 10 × 10 ones corresponding to the recording electrodes.
source: The different modules are placed on a square 24 × 24 grid with the central 10 × 10 ones corresponding to the recording electrodes (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of the model setup, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Capaday et al., 2009 report a uniform distribution of boutons along horizontal axons, not a patchy one.
source: Notably, Capaday et al., 2009 report a uniform distribution of boutons along horizontal axons, not a patchy one.
evidence: This is a specific finding from Capaday et al., 2009.

claim: A relatively slow propagation speed (∼30 cm/s) along unmyelinated horizontal axons in the monkey cortex has been reported in previous works.
source: A relatively slow propagation speed (∼30 cm/s) along unmyelinated horizontal axons in the monkey cortex has been reported in previous works (González-Burgos et al., 2000; Girard et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to González-Burgos et al., 2000 and Girard et al., 2001.

claim: A comparable speed has been found for horizontal connections in the rat visual cortex.
source: A comparable speed has been found for horizontal connections in the rat visual cortex (Lohmann and Rörig, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lohmann and Rörig, 1994.

claim: With other parameters fixed, a steady firing rate state in which excitatory and inhibitory populations fire at rEs and rIs is unstable when the strength of recurrent disynaptic self-inhibition β becomes larger than a threshold value.
source: With other parameters fixed, a steady firing rate state in which excitatory and inhibitory populations fire at rEs and rIs is unstable when the strength of recurrent disynaptic self-inhibition β becomes larger than a threshold value.
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical analysis of the model.

claim: When recurrent excitation increases, the oscillation frequency decreases.
source: When recurrent excitation increases, the oscillation frequency decreases.
evidence: This is an observation from the model analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Propagation delays displace the bifurcation lines but do not change much how the oscillation frequency depends on recurrent excitation.
source: As seen in Figure 1b, propagation delays displace the bifurcation lines but do not change much how the oscillation frequency depends on recurrent excitation.
evidence: This is an observation from the model analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: For the ON model, the network oscillates regularly when recurrent inhibition is stronger than the critical value.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1c and d, for recurrent inhibition stronger than the critical value, the ON model oscillates regularly.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: For the SN model with lower recurrent inhibition, the firing rates of the excitatory and inhibitory populations steadily fire at constant rates.
source: For a lower value of recurrent inhibition (SN model), the firing rates of the excitatory and inhibitory populations steadily fire at constant rates.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations.

claim: When perturbed away from steady rates, the SN model firing rates relax to their stationary values in an oscillatory fashion, transiently exhibiting beta oscillations.
source: When perturbed away from these rates, the firing rates relax to their stationary values in an oscillatory fashion, transiently exhibiting beta oscillations.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations.

claim: When the external input on the inhibitory neurons is increased, their steady firing rate and the steady firing rate of the excitatory population both decrease for a large range of the external input current.
source: Interestingly, when the external input on the inhibitory neurons is increased, their steady firing rate and the steady firing rate of the excitatory population both decrease for a large range of the external input current.
evidence: This is an observation from model analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The 'paradoxical suppression of inhibition' is typical of inhibition-stabilized networks and is observed in many cortical areas including motor cortex.
source: This 'paradoxical suppression of inhibition' (Tsodyks et al., 1997) is typical of inhibition-stabilized networks and is observed in many cortical areas (Ozeki et al., 2009; Sanzeni et al., 2020) including motor cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tsodyks et al., 1997; Ozeki et al., 2009; and Sanzeni et al., 2020.

claim: The SN model exhibits paradoxical suppression of inhibition because it is only when recurrent excitation is large that its frequency of oscillation is in the beta range.
source: It arises in the SN model because it is only when recurrent excitation is large, as measured by the parameter α, that its frequency of oscillation is in the beta range (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an explanation based on model analysis with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: All networks with α>1 cannot stably fire at moderate rates without being stabilized by inhibition.
source: Namely all networks with α>1 cannot stably fire at moderate rates without being stabilized by inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: External inputs suppress beta oscillations in motor cortex.
source: This conforms to the early observation (Jasper and Penfield, 1949; Penfield, 1954) that external inputs suppress beta oscillations in motor cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jasper and Penfield, 1949 and Penfield, 1954.

claim: When the external input strength on the SN model varies in time, beta oscillations are dampened at varying rates, leading to waxing and waning of their amplitudes.
source: When the external input strength on the SN model varies in time, its operating point moves relative to the bifurcation line and correspondingly, beta oscillations are dampened at varying rates. This leads to waxing and waning of their amplitudes as shown in Figure 1g and h.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations shown in Figure 1g and h.

claim: The average power of beta oscillations changes on a second time scale with different phases of movement.
source: As confirmed in several later studies (see, e.g., Feingold et al., 2015), the average power of beta oscillations changes on a second time scale with different phases of movement, for example, preparation, execution, and post-execution periods.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feingold et al., 2015.

claim: Within individual trials, the amplitude of beta oscillations fluctuates on much shorter time scales with brief bursts of elevated amplitudes of ∼100 ms duration.
source: Within individual trials, the amplitude of beta oscillations fluctuates on much shorter time scales with brief bursts of elevated amplitudes of ∼100 ms duration.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from experimental data.

claim: The model accurately reproduces the statistics of recording data when external inputs are correlated on a short time scale (25 ms) and have two different components, one that targets the motor cortex locally and another one that targets it in a global and synchronized way.
source: We show that the model accurately reproduces the statistics of recording data when these external inputs are correlated on a short time scale (25 ms) and have two different components, one that targets the motor cortex locally and another one that targets it in a global and synchronized way.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model simulations to experimental data.

claim: The model reproduces the distribution of beta burst durations.
source: The model reproduces the distribution of beta burst durations, the proportion of the different observed wave types, and wave speeds, which we show not to be linked to axonal propagation speed.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model simulations to experimental data.

claim: The model reproduces the proportion of the different observed wave types.
source: The model reproduces the distribution of beta burst durations, the proportion of the different observed wave types, and wave speeds, which we show not to be linked to axonal propagation speed.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model simulations to experimental data.

claim: Wave speeds are not linked to axonal propagation speed.
source: The model reproduces the distribution of beta burst durations, the proportion of the different observed wave types, and wave speeds, which we show not to be linked to axonal propagation speed.
evidence: This is a finding from model analysis.

claim: When the long-range connectivity or the local input targets are anisotropic, traveling waves are found to preferentially propagate along the axis where connectivity decays the fastest.
source: When the long-range connectivity or the local input targets are anisotropic, traveling waves are found to preferentially propagate along the axis where connectivity decays the fastest.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations with anisotropic connectivity.

claim: Traveling waves in motor cortex are the reflection of the dephasing by external inputs, putatively of thalamic origin, of an oscillatory activity that would otherwise be spatially synchronized by recurrent connectivity.
source: Different from previously proposed mechanistic explanations, the model suggests that traveling waves in motor cortex are the reflection of the dephasing by external inputs, putatively of thalamic origin, of an oscillatory activity that would otherwise be spatially synchronized by recurrent connectivity.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation proposed by the authors based on model behavior.

claim: The correlation between two neighboring electrodes is lower than the autocorrelation of a single-electrode LFP, but is comparable to the correlation between more distant electrodes.
source: As shown in Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g, the correlation between two neighboring electrodes is lower than the autocorrelation of a single-electrode LFP, namely, its variance, but is comparable to the correlation between more distant electrodes.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Part of the LFP signal is strongly synchronized between distant electrodes.
source: Namely, part of the LFP signal is strongly synchronized between distant electrodes.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation patterns observed in the data.

claim: When the external inputs are almost equally split between local and global contributions, the model correlations are comparable to the experimental ones.
source: As shown in Figure 2o, it is only when the external inputs are almost equally split between local and global contributions that the model correlations are comparable to the experimental ones.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model simulations to experimental data shown in Figure 2o.

claim: For monkey L, the value c=0.4 provides the best match between model and experimental correlations.
source: For monkey L (N), the value c=0.4 (c=0.3) is found to provide the best match.
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the model to experimental data.

claim: For monkey N, the value c=0.3 provides the best match between model and experimental correlations.
source: For monkey L (N), the value c=0.4 (c=0.3) is found to provide the best match.
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the model to experimental data.

claim: Several groups have reported traveling waves on the motor cortex during the preparatory phase of the movement in instructed-delay reaching tasks.
source: Several groups have reported traveling waves on the motor cortex during the preparatory phase of the movement in instructed-delay reaching tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings.

claim: In the early study of Rubino et al., 2006, planar waves of beta oscillations in multielectrode LFP recordings were described.
source: In the early study of Rubino et al., 2006, planar waves of beta oscillations in multielectrode LFP recordings were described.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rubino et al., 2006.

claim: Later works classified the spatio-temporal beta oscillations recorded by multielectrode arrays into different states.
source: Later works (Rule et al., 2018; Denker et al., 2018) have classified the spatio-temporal beta oscillations recorded by multielectrode arrays into different states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rule et al., 2018 and Denker et al., 2018.

claim: The classification scheme distinguishes periods with planar (Pla.) or radial (Rad.) waves, as well as globally synchronized (Syn.) episodes and more random (Ran.) appearing states.
source: Here, we use the data of Brochier et al., 2018 and closely follow the classification scheme proposed by these authors (Denker et al., 2018), distinguishing periods with planar (Pla.) or radial (Rad.) waves, as well as globally synchronized (Syn.) episodes and more random (Ran.) appearing states.
evidence: This is a description of the classification method used, based on Denker et al., 2018.

claim: The median planar wave speed is about 30 cm/s.
source: The median planar wave speed is about 30 cm/s but it should be noted that the distribution includes also events with much smaller velocities.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The distribution of planar wave speeds includes events with much smaller velocities than the median.
source: The median planar wave speed is about 30 cm/s but it should be noted that the distribution includes also events with much smaller velocities.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data analysis.

claim: In the SN model, the input fluctuations promote oscillations.
source: In the SN model, the input fluctuations promote oscillations.
evidence: This is an observation from model behavior.

claim: Increasing the noise amplitude first increases the proportion of synchronized activity and the propagation speed of planar waves in the SN model.
source: Thus, increasing the noise amplitude first increases the proportion of synchronized activity and the propagation speed of planar waves.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: At higher noise amplitudes, the desynchronizing effect of noise counteracts its oscillation-promoting effect and the wave speed decreases with increasing input amplitude in the SN model.
source: At higher noise amplitudes, the desynchronizing effect of noise counteracts its oscillation-promoting effect and the wave speed decreases with increasing input amplitude.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations.

claim: For the ON model, the oscillatory activity is self-generated and the oscillations between different modules are well-synchronized without fluctuating inputs.
source: In this case, the oscillatory activity is self-generated and the oscillations between different modules are well-synchronized without fluctuating inputs.
evidence: This is a description of the ON model behavior.

claim: In the ON model, the local inputs tend to desynchronize the different modules and create oscillatory phase differences between them.
source: The local inputs tend to desynchronize the different modules and create oscillatory phase differences between them.
evidence: This is an observation from model behavior.

claim: The speed of planar waves decreases with increasing νext in the ON model.
source: The speed of planar waves that is inversely proportional to the magnitude of phase gradients (Equation 1) also decreases.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations.

claim: The model and the simulation results suggest that the observed spatio-temporal patterns arise from the opposing effects of synchronization by long-range excitatory connectivity and global inputs and desynchronization by local inputs and the intrinsic stochasticity arising from the finite number of neurons in each module.
source: The model and the simulation results suggest that the observed spatio-temporal patterns arise from the opposing effects of synchronization by long-range excitatory connectivity and global inputs and desynchronization by local inputs and the intrinsic stochasticity arising from the finite number of neurons in each module.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation proposed by the authors based on model behavior.

claim: Results comparable to the reference model can only be obtained when the number of neurons per module is lowered to N=200 in simulations without local inputs.
source: Results comparable to our reference model can only be obtained when the number of neurons per module is lowered to N=200 (Figure 3—figure supplement 9a–d).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claim: N=200 would be quite a low number for the 0.1-0.2 mm2 area of motor cortex that each module is meant to represent.
source: This of course would be quite a low number for the 0.1-0.2 mm2 area of motor cortex that each module is meant to represent, even if restricted to the cortical layers (e.g., II/III) where the dynamics could mainly take place.
evidence: This is a reasoning based on known cortical anatomy.

claim: Shuffling entirely suppresses the appearance of planar waves in both simulations and experimental recordings.
source: More interestingly, shuffling entirely suppresses the appearance of planar waves.
evidence: This is a finding from data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 10.

claim: The spatial correlation of different electrode signals, a reflection of the underlying long-range connectivity, is crucial for the appearance of planar waves.
source: Therefore, the spatial correlation of different electrode signals, a reflection of the underlying long-range connectivity, is crucial for the appearance of planar waves.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the shuffling analysis.

claim: The mean speeds of planar waves in the recordings and in the model are of a few tens of cm/s.
source: The mean speeds of planar waves in the recordings and in the model are of a few tens of cm/s (Figure 3e and k and Figure 3—figure supplement 2e and k), which is comparable to the propagation speed along non-myelinated horizontal fibers (González-Burgos et al., 2000; Girard et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an observation from both experimental data and model simulations, with citation to González-Burgos et al., 2000 and Girard et al., 2001.

claim: The mean planar wave speed is not tightly linked to axonal propagation speed.
source: One might thus think that both are tightly linked. This is actually not the case.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model analysis comparing cases with and without propagation delays.

claim: An equally good agreement with the recording data can be found in the model in the absence of propagation delay (D=0).
source: An equally good agreement with the recording data can be found in the model in the absence of propagation delay, that is, for D=0.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 11.

claim: When long-range excitatory connections are absent (l=0), both synchronized states and planar waves are absent and replaced by random states.
source: First, when long-range excitatory connections are absent (l=0), both synchronized states and planar waves are absent and replaced by random states (Figure 3—figure supplement 12a).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 12a.

claim: Long-range excitatory connections are required for planar wave existence.
source: This confirms that long-range excitatory connections are required for planar wave existence.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model simulations with l=0.

claim: When l is halved compared to the reference model, both synchronized states and planar waves exist but in reduced proportions.
source: Second, when l is halved (Figure 3—figure supplement 12b) as compared to the reference model of Figure 3 (i.e., l=1 in module distance units or 400μm in real units), both synchronized states and planar waves exist but in reduced proportions as compared to the reference case.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 12b.

claim: The speed of planar waves is strongly reduced when l is halved.
source: The speed of planar waves is also strongly reduced.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations.

claim: When l is increased by 50% compared to the reference model, synchronization between distant modules is increased, the synchronized regime prevails and planar wave occurrence is reduced.
source: Finally, when l is increased by 50% (Figure 3—figure supplement 12c) as compared to the reference model, synchronization between distant modules is increased, the synchronized regime prevails and planar wave occurrence is reduced.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 12c.

claim: Planar waves predominantly arise from synchronized states.
source: It is interesting that planar waves predominantly arise from synchronized states and moreover that synchronized states tend to persist in the background of planar waves.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations.

claim: The global input to the whole network is shifted to negative values before the appearance of a planar wave.
source: The global input to the whole network is found to be shifted to negative values before the appearance of a planar wave (Figure 4d), effectively reducing the drive to both the excitatory and the inhibitory populations of all modules and pushing the network towards its self-sustained oscillating regime (see Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a finding from model analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Injection of negative current steps resulted in a 50% increase of the number of planar wave episodes.
source: The injection of these current steps resulted in a 50% increase of the number of planar wave episodes (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is a finding from model perturbation experiments shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Injection of steps with the opposite sign of the injected current strongly reduced the appearance of planar waves.
source: This was not simply a result of the perturbation of the network since injection of steps with the opposite sign of the injected current on the contrary strongly reduced the appearance of planar waves (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is a finding from model perturbation experiments shown in Figure 4g.

claim: It was reported by Rubino et al., 2006 that waves tend to propagate along preferred axes on the cortical surface with respect to sulcal landmarks.
source: However, it was reported by Rubino et al., 2006 that waves tend to propagate along preferred axes on the cortical surface with respect to sulcal landmarks and that the orientation of the preferred axes of propagation also vary between different regions, for example, between primary motor cortex and dorsal premotor cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rubino et al., 2006.

claim: The orientation of the preferred axes of wave propagation vary between different regions, for example, between primary motor cortex and dorsal premotor cortex.
source: However, it was reported by Rubino et al., 2006 that waves tend to propagate along preferred axes on the cortical surface with respect to sulcal landmarks and that the orientation of the preferred axes of propagation also vary between different regions, for example, between primary motor cortex and dorsal premotor cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rubino et al., 2006.

claim: When connections are anisotropic with twice longer range in the y-direction than in the x-direction, there is a large predominance of waves observed to propagate along the x-axis.
source: Figure 5f shows the measured distribution of the directions along which planar waves propagate when connections are anisotropic. The fractions of waves propagating along the x- and y-axis are clearly different. There is a large predominance of waves observed to propagate along the x-axis, namely, along the axis where the connectivity is shorter range.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations with anisotropic connectivity shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Longer-range connectivity promotes longer-range synchronization along the y-axis and synchronized states.
source: Longer-range connectivity promotes longer-range synchronization along the y-axis and synchronized states.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed wave propagation pattern based on model behavior.

claim: The weaker connectivity along the x-axis allows for the formation of the larger phase gradients along the x-axis and planar waves.
source: The weaker connectivity along the x-axis allows for the formation of the larger phase gradients along the x-axis and planar waves.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed wave propagation pattern based on model behavior.

claim: Anisotropic targeting of local inputs produces a clear anisotropy in the distribution of planar wave propagation directions.
source: This anisotropic targeting of local inputs produces a clear anisotropy in the distribution of planar wave propagation directions, as shown in Figure 5l.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations with anisotropic local inputs shown in Figure 5l.

claim: Planar waves preferentially propagate along the x-axis where the inputs are confined to a narrower region and gradients in the phase of the oscillatory activity are more easily produced.
source: Planar waves preferentially propagate along the x-axis where the inputs are confined to a narrower region and gradients in the phase of the oscillatory activity are more easily produced.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed wave propagation pattern based on model behavior.

claim: Both anisotropy in connectivity and in the targets of local inputs can produce an anisotropy in wave speed direction.
source: Thus, both anisotropy in connectivity and in the targets of local inputs can produce an anisotropy in wave speed direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations with different types of anisotropy.

claim: Gatter et al., 1978 reported a more spatially extended connectivity in layers 2/3 and 5 of motor cortex in non-human primates in the rostro-caudal direction.
source: However, Gatter et al., 1978 reported a more spatially extended connectivity in layers 2/3 and 5 of motor cortex in non-human primates in the rostro-caudal direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gatter et al., 1978.

claim: Rubino et al., 2006 found that planar waves predominantly propagated along the rostro-caudal axis.
source: Rubino et al., 2006 found that planar waves predominantly propagated along the same rostro-caudal axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rubino et al., 2006.

claim: The findings argue against connectivity anisotropy being the dominant factor determining planar wave speed direction.
source: Given our results, this argues against connectivity anisotropy being the dominant factor determining planar wave speed direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing model predictions with experimental observations.

claim: The model suggests that local input targets are more spread out along the medio-lateral dimension.
source: It remains to be investigated whether local input targets are more spread out along the medio-lateral dimension, as the model suggests.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that requires experimental testing.

claim: The model builds on previous works describing beta oscillations in motor cortex as arising from recurrent interactions between excitatory and inhibitory populations.
source: This builds on previous works describing beta oscillations in motor cortex as arising from recurrent interactions between excitatory and inhibitory populations (Pavlides et al., 2015; Sherman et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pavlides et al., 2015; Sherman et al., 2016; and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: The model of Sherman et al., 2016 includes two layers of hundred multi-compartment spiking neurons to approximately take into account the layered structure of the cortex and allow a detailed comparison with MEG signals.
source: Of note, the model of a single E-I module of Sherman et al., 2016 includes two layers of hundred multi-compartment spiking neurons to approximately take into account the layered structure of the cortex and allow a detailed comparison with MEG signals.
evidence: This is a description of the Sherman et al., 2016 model.

claim: The present model uses a simpler description of an E-I module but goes beyond previous works by taking into account long-range interactions and analyzing the resulting spatio-temporal patterns.
source: In a complementary fashion, our model uses a simpler description of an E-I module but goes beyond these previous works by taking into account long-range interactions and analyzing the resulting spatio-temporal patterns.
evidence: This is a description of how the present model differs from previous work.

claim: The well-known oscillatory instability of coupled E-I networks is not qualitatively modified by the presence of long-range connections.
source: The well-known oscillatory instability of coupled E-I networks is not qualitatively modified by the presence of long-range connections and the model displays an instability leading to sustained oscillatory behavior.
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical analysis of the model.

claim: These oscillations occur at beta frequency for adequate synaptic parameters.
source: These oscillations occur at beta frequency for adequate synaptic parameters.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Comparison with available data has led to the conclusion that the motor cortex operates close to the beta oscillatory instability line under strong fluctuating inputs from other areas.
source: Comparison with available data has led us to conclude that the motor cortex operates close to this beta oscillatory instability line under strong fluctuating inputs from other areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing model behavior to experimental data.

claim: A similar proximity of an oscillatory regime has been proposed for the bursts of beta oscillations in the basal ganglia using different models.
source: A similar proximity of an oscillatory regime has been proposed for the bursts of beta oscillations in the basal ganglia using different models (Rubchinsky et al., 2012; Bahuguna et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rubchinsky et al., 2012 and Bahuguna et al., 2020.

claim: The observed power enhancement on the low frequency-side of the beta peak requires that the time correlation of external inputs is not too short on a 10 ms scale.
source: The observed power enhancement on the low frequency-side of the beta peak requires that their time correlation is not too short on a 10 ms scale while the duration of the observed oscillation bursts requires that it is not too long on the same time scale.
evidence: This is a constraint on model parameters derived from comparison with experimental data.

claim: The duration of the observed oscillation bursts requires that the time correlation of external inputs is not too long on a 10 ms scale.
source: The observed power enhancement on the low frequency-side of the beta peak requires that their time correlation is not too short on a 10 ms scale while the duration of the observed oscillation bursts requires that it is not too long on the same time scale.
evidence: This is a constraint on model parameters derived from comparison with experimental data.

claim: The external input amplitude should be sufficiently large to significantly modify the LFP characteristics above the background of intrinsic local fluctuations.
source: In an analogous way, the external input amplitude should be, on the one hand, sufficiently large to significantly modify the LFP characteristics above the background of intrinsic local fluctuations arising from the finite number of neurons sampled by each electrode.
evidence: This is a constraint on model parameters derived from comparison with experimental data.

claim: The external input amplitude should be small enough to preserve the harmonicity of beta oscillations, as indicated by the absence of a significant secondary 50–60 Hz peak in the LFP spectra.
source: On the other hand, it should be small enough to preserve the harmonicity of beta oscillations, as indicated by the absence of a significant secondary 50–60 Hz peak in the LFP spectra.
evidence: This is a constraint on model parameters derived from comparison with experimental data.

claim: The motor cortex receives inputs that target local areas but also synchronous inputs that target it more globally.
source: The spatial correlation of beta oscillations at the millimeter distance scale has furthermore led us to suggest that the motor cortex receives inputs that target local areas but also synchronous inputs that target it more globally.
evidence: This is a proposal based on comparison with experimental data.

claim: Under the proposed input conditions, traveling waves of different kinds are observed that resemble those recorded in vivo both in their repartition between the different wave types and their speeds of propagation.
source: Under these conditions, traveling waves of different kinds are observed that resemble those recorded in vivo both in their repartition between the different wave types and their speeds of propagation.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model simulations to experimental data.

claim: Characterization of the inputs onto motor cortex during movement preparation is needed to test the theoretical predictions.
source: Characterization of the inputs onto motor cortex during movement preparation is needed to test these theoretical predictions.
evidence: This is a statement about future experimental work needed to validate the model.

claim: Propagating waves of neural activity have been observed in different contexts.
source: Propagating waves of neural activity have been observed in different contexts (Ermentrout and Kleinfeld, 2001; Muller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ermentrout and Kleinfeld, 2001 and Muller et al., 2018.

claim: Some propagating waves are unrelated to neural oscillations such as subthreshold waves or propagation of spiking activity in visual cortex.
source: Some are unrelated to neural oscillations such as subthreshold waves (Bringuier et al., 1999) or propagation of spiking activity in visual cortex (Davis et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bringuier et al., 1999 and Davis et al., 2020.

claim: Other propagating waves are based on oscillatory activity with proposed mechanisms relying on a gradient of frequencies or structural sequences of activation.
source: Others are based on oscillatory activity with proposed mechanisms relying on a gradient of frequencies (Ermentrout et al., 1998) or structural sequences of activation (Muller et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ermentrout et al., 1998 and Muller et al., 2016.

claim: The traveling waves in the present model are based on the existence of oscillations since they are a reflection of different phases of oscillation at different positions on motor cortex.
source: They are obviously based on the existence of oscillations since the traveling waves are a reflection of different phases of oscillation at different positions on motor cortex.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism underlying traveling waves in the model.

claim: The model includes structural connectivity that tends to synchronize oscillations at different positions, but the stochastic external inputs play an essential role in creating dephasings between different locations.
source: The model we have developed here includes structural connectivity that tends to synchronize oscillations at different positions, but the stochastic external inputs play an essential role in creating dephasings between different locations.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism underlying traveling waves in the model.

claim: The wave propagation speeds are found to be rather low and distributed in the few tens of cm/s.
source: The wave propagation speeds are found to be rather low and distributed in the few tens of cm/s.
evidence: This is an observation from model simulations.

claim: The observed speeds of the oscillatory waves of activity are set by the oscillatory frequency and by the dephasings produced by the external inputs in the recorded area.
source: In the present context, the observed speeds of the oscillatory waves of activity are set by the oscillatory frequency and by the dephasings produced by the external inputs in the recorded area.
evidence: This is an explanation of what determines wave speeds in the model.

claim: The existence of a global component of external inputs appears consistent with the presence of global inhibition in motor cortex during movement preparation.
source: The existence of a global component appears consistent with the presence of global inhibition in motor cortex during movement preparation (Greenhouse et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greenhouse et al., 2015.

claim: The model 'external inputs' could represent direct inputs from different neural structures, including other cortical areas such as frontal and parietal cortex, and extra-cortical ones like the thalamus, or a mixture of the two.
source: The model 'external inputs' could represent direct inputs from different neural structures, including other cortical areas such as frontal and parietal cortex (Davare et al., 2011), and extra-cortical ones like the thalamus (Hooks et al., 2013), or a mixture of the two.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological sources of model inputs, with citations to Davare et al., 2011 and Hooks et al., 2013.

claim: The known thalamo-cortical connectivity makes the thalamus a privileged candidate for the origin of, at least, part of the external inputs.
source: The known thalamo-cortical connectivity (Jones, 2001) makes the thalamus a privileged candidate for the origin of, at least, part of these external inputs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known anatomy, with citation to Jones, 2001.

claim: The described diffused connectivity from calbindin-positive matrix neurons could be the source of global inputs while core parvalbumin-positive neurons could be the source of local inputs.
source: Indeed the described diffused connectivity from calbindin-positive matrix neurons could be the source of our global inputs while core parvalbumin-positive neurons could be the source of our local inputs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological sources of different input types based on known thalamic cell types.

claim: The observed anisotropy of wave propagation is linked to the anisotropy of local input targets, with the specific prediction that traveling waves of oscillatory activity are predominantly observed orthogonal to the axis where they are more spread out.
source: We have moreover suggested that the observed anisotropy of wave propagation is linked to the anisotropy of local input targets, with the specific prediction that traveling waves of oscillatory activity are predominantly observed orthogonal to the axis where they are more spread out.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that requires experimental testing.

claim: The model suggests that inputs to the motor cortex play an important role in the generation of beta oscillations and of spatio-temporal patterns during movement preparation.
source: The model suggests that inputs to the motor cortex play an important role in the generation of beta oscillations and of spatio-temporal patterns during movement preparation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: Traveling waves have been shown to carry information about the subsequent movement.
source: Indeed, traveling waves have been shown to carry information about the subsequent movement (Rubino et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rubino et al., 2006.

claim: Movement preparation is presently viewed, in a dynamical systems perspective, as taking place in a subspace orthogonal to the dynamics of the movement itself and producing the proper initial condition for it.
source: Movement preparation is presently viewed, in a dynamical systems perspective, as taking place in a subspace orthogonal to the dynamics of the movement itself and producing the proper initial condition for it (Kaufman et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018; Zimnik and Churchland, 2021; Inagaki et al., 2022; Bachschmid-Romano et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaufman et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018; Zimnik and Churchland, 2021; Inagaki et al., 2022; and Bachschmid-Romano et al., 2022.

claim: Beta oscillations and their associated timescale are absent from the current dynamical systems description of movement preparation.
source: Beta oscillations and their associated timescale are however absent from this description.
evidence: This is an observation about the current state of the field.
